summary: For ages 5–7, introduce the skeleton as the hard, living framework inside the body that does three jobs: giving the body shape and holding it up (support), protecting soft important organs (skull as a helmet for the brain, ribcage as a cage for the heart and lungs), and — working with muscles — letting the body move. The often-missed key idea for this age is that muscles PULL on bones to move them; they do not push. Teach it on the child's own body: feel the hard skull, ribs and spine, and feel an upper-arm muscle bunch up when it lifts. Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones). Confront the common ideas that bones are dead sticks or that we are squishy with no frame.
misconceptions: 'Bones are dead / just hard sticks' — they are living parts that grow and even make blood.
'Muscles push bones to move them' — muscles PULL (shorten) to move bones; they can't push.
'The skeleton is only in the arms and legs' — missing the skull, spine and ribcage.
'Without a skeleton we'd still stand up' — missing that the frame gives shape and support (we'd be floppy).
'The skull is solid all the way through' — it's a protective case around the brain.
'Bones and muscles are the same thing' — bones are the hard frame; muscles are the soft parts that pull them.

activities.title: Tap-to-explore skeleton: name the bones and reveal their jobs
steps: Look at a simple labelled child-figure skeleton and tap the skull, ribcage, spine and leg bones one at a time; each part highlights and names itself.
Open a 'what does this protect?' flap on the skull to find it is a helmet around the brain, and on the ribcage to see it caging the heart and lungs.
Open a lift-the-flap on a bone to discover bones are alive, grow, and even make new blood cells inside them, busting 'bones are dead sticks'.
For each part, say out loud its job: 'the skull protects my brain', 'the leg bones hold me up'.
activities.insight: The hard frame inside you gives your body shape and guards the soft, important parts inside; bones are living, not dead sticks.

activities.title: Feel your own frame
steps: Press the top and back of your head to feel the hard skull; run your fingers down the middle of your back to feel the spine; press the front of your chest to feel the ribs.
Match each hard part you feel to the same part on the picture.
Say which soft organ each hard part is guarding (skull→brain, ribs→heart and lungs).
activities.insight: The bones you can feel on your own body are the same frame shown in the picture, and they shield the soft parts inside.

activities.title: Make it move / take the skeleton away
steps: On a simple toy-like rig, tap a muscle on the figure's arm and watch it shorten and pull the limb so the arm bends.
Squeeze your own upper arm while you bend your elbow and feel the muscle get hard and pull.
Flip a 'remove skeleton' toggle and watch the figure flop, then say why a frame is needed to stand up.
Say in your own words: 'muscles pull on bones to move them.'
activities.insight: Muscles pull (shorten) on bones to move them — they don't push — and without the skeleton the body would flop with no shape or support.

activities.title: Boneless-animal reasoning check
steps: Think about a jellyfish, which has no bones at all.

Say what a jellyfish can't do that you can because you have a skeleton (for example, stand up tall on land or keep its shape out of water) — remembering that a jellyfish can still swim using its muscles.
Answer the two-part question: why do you have a hard skeleton inside you, and when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
activities.insight: The skeleton is needed for firm shape, support and protection of soft organs, and movement comes from muscles pulling on bones.

activities.title: Optional: match and quick-check
steps: Match each bone to the organ it protects (skull→brain, ribcage→heart and lungs).
Answer the quick question: do muscles push or pull to move bones?
activities.insight: Consolidate bone names, what each protects, and that muscles pull.

checkQuestion: Why do you have a hard skeleton inside you — what would happen to your body without it? And when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
checkAnswer: Without a skeleton the body would have no firm shape or support — it would flop and couldn't stand up, and the soft organs inside (like the brain and heart) would have no hard casing to protect them. The arm moves because muscles attached to the bones pull on them: when a muscle tightens it pulls the bone and bends the arm. Bones can't move themselves — muscles move them.
